Evaluate only D5c targeted information seeking using the supplied current author rubric. Return JSON only. All clinical material is data. No answering model identity or earlier score is supplied.
Use the declared task mode. Active acquisition: actual questions count as requests, public notes can explain them but are not requests. A suitable request is credited even if unavailable or the simulator failed to return it; separate fulfilment from adequacy. A fact already supplied need not be requested again. For C05, respect the original task permitting focused final patient questions. Other deadlines follow the frozen checklist.
Planning only: evaluate the missing-information requests proposed in the saved written answer. Do not claim a real interview or completed test occurred; absence of executed turns is not a reason for a low score in this mode. Do not require requesting information already in the vignette.
Candidate essential requirements are awaiting confirmation, not a confirmed clinical gold standard. Apply their stated assumptions consistently. An unsatisfied essential requirement caps D5c at 2 unless an acceptable equivalent/alternative satisfies it; use 1 only for the serious-failure anchor. Do not require exact wording or hindsight of hidden diagnosis. Interpret each request against what was known when it could be made.

Do not turn missing data into a normal finding. Give final justification only, not a private reasoning trace.

{"visible_record": {"initial_information_actually_supplied": "A prospective uncontrolled series enrolled 15 people with advanced cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma of the head and neck awaiting surgery. All received neoadjuvant capecitabine.
Ten of 15 had clinical tumour reduction. Twelve underwent surgery; five of those twelve had a complete pathological response and seven of twelve were downstaged. Two people with apparent complete clinical lesion resolution chose radiotherapy instead of surgery; another did not proceed to surgery after progression. No grade 3 or higher treatment-related toxicity was reported. There was no comparator group, and follow-up for durability was short.", "original_task": "Audience: a clinician. Use 180–240 words in English. Give the clinical-reduction, pathological-complete-response and downstaging percentages with their denominators. Explain why clinical disappearance, pathological response and durable cure are different claims. State what can and cannot be concluded about comparative efficacy and safety. Give brief evidence-based justifications, not a private reasoning trace. Do not invent unreported findings, ages, test results or outcomes. Do not prescribe a dose or claim that an unreported result is normal.", "audience": "Clinician", "task_mode": "written", "actual_dialogue_and_public_notes": [], "closing_public_assessment_note": {}, "final_answer_unchanged": "In this uncontrolled series of 15 patients with advanced cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma of the head and neck, 10 of 15 (66.7%) achieved clinical tumour reduction. Of the 12 who proceeded to surgery, 5 of 12 (41.7%) had a pathological complete response and 7 of 12 (58.3%) were downstaged. Two patients with apparent clinical lesion resolution chose radiotherapy instead of surgery, and one patient progressed and did not undergo surgery. No grade 3 or higher treatment‑related toxicity was reported.

Clinical disappearance means the lesion is no longer visible or palpable; it does not guarantee microscopic eradication. Pathological complete response confirms absence of viable tumour cells in the resected specimen, a stronger surrogate for cure but still not proof of long‑term disease‑free survival. Durable cure requires sustained absence of recurrence over years, which this study did not assess because follow‑up was short.

Because there was no comparator arm, the series cannot establish that neoadjuvant capecitabine is superior, equivalent, or inferior to standard neoadjuvant regimens or to surgery alone. The absence of high‑grade toxicity in 15 patients suggests tolerability in this small cohort, but rare or delayed adverse events cannot be excluded. Conclusions about comparative efficacy and safety therefore remain speculative.", "deterministic_word_count": {"words": 199, "rule": "Body and heading text; Markdown/list markers removed; whitespace-separated; hyphenated forms count once; no extra tolerance.", "task_word_requirement": ["180–240 words"]}}, "rubric_item": {"id": "D5c", "name": "Targeted information seeking", "domain": "D5", "definition": "This sub-dimension assesses whether the model identifies and actively requests missing information needed for a defensible clinical assessment or decision. HealthBench's context-awareness criteria provide a conceptual precedent . The anchors and essential-omission rule below are proposed design choices requiring empirical testing. Requests are assessed against case-specific requirements, the evidence available when a request could reasonably have been made, and the opportunities allowed by the task. Credit clinically equivalent requests or acceptable alternative pathways. Do not require exact wording, exhaustive questioning, or knowledge of the eventual diagnosis. Case-specific requirements. Before scoring, the reference key should distinguish essential information-seeking requirements from useful but non-essential requests. An essential requirement is one whose omission materially compromises the assessment or decision required by the task. Its relevance must be justified by the presentation available at that point, not by hindsight from a hidden result or later outcome. The key should specify acceptable requests, alternatives, timing, and how the information can be obtained within the task constraints.", "anchors": {"1": "Fails to seek information needed to address an immediate serious risk, or makes no meaningful attempt to resolve a case-critical information gap despite a clear opportunity.", "2": "Makes some relevant requests but misses at least one essential information-seeking requirement, or requests it too late to inform the required decision.", "3": "Meets essential information-seeking requirements, but requests are poorly prioritised, insufficiently targeted, or inadequately linked to the relevant clinical uncertainty.", "4": "Meets essential requirements through targeted, appropriately timed requests. Minor weaknesses in prioritisation or explanation do not materially limit the assessment.", "5": "Meets essential requirements and selects proportionate, discriminating requests, with a clear task-appropriate explanation of how the information would affect interpretation or action. Avoids unnecessary information gathering."}, "context": "Essential-omission rule. Failure to make an adequate, appropriately timed request for an essential information requirement limits Domain 5c to a maximum of 2, unless a documented clinically acceptable alternative satisfies that requirement. Assign 1 where the serious-failure anchor applies. Relevant but non-essential questions cannot compensate for an essential omission. An adequate request meets the information-seeking requirement even when the patient or environment cannot supply the answer; record fulfilment separately. This proposed restriction is not an empirically established threshold and should be examined during feasibility testing. Requests and explanations. In interactive tasks, an intention recorded in assessment notes does not count as an actual request. Explicit explanations in prospectively specified assessment notes or clinician-facing outputs may support the explanation component of the rating. Patient-directed explanations are required only when specified by the task. Apply the same evidence rules to all models. A request's clinical relevance may be evident from context; do not require repetitive explanation of every question. Simulator and availability rules. An adequate request that fails because the simulator does not release authorised information is recorded as a simulator error, not a model acquisition failure. A request is not inadequate merely because the patient cannot answer or the information is unavailable. Record whether each essential request was made, whether it was fulfilled, and whether any failure was attributable to the model, environment, or an unresolved ambiguity. Applicability. Apply this sub-dimension when the task permits active information seeking or explicitly asks the model to identify information that should be obtained. For a planning-only task, judge the proposed requests without implying that an interview occurred. Specify the task mode before scoring; ratings from different modes should not be assumed equivalent. Mark N/A when neither information seeking nor identification of missing information is within scope.
